papers.title: Differentiability of the shape function in the planar corner growth model
papers.label: arXiv:2611.33433v1

summary.one_liner: The paper proves that the time-constant (shape) function of planar directed last-passage percolation with general i.i.d. real weights is differentiable on the open first quadrant, under moment conditions on the weights, and gives a Lean-formalized proof adapted from an AI-assisted first-passage percolation argument.
summary.plain: The paper studies a random growth model where paths collect random weights and the maximum total weight from a corner grows in a predictable way. It shows that the function describing this growth speed, as the direction changes, is smooth (differentiable) in the open first quadrant, provided the weights have enough finite moments. The proof is also written and checked in the Lean proof assistant, and it was adapted from an AI-assisted proof for a related model.
summary.why: Whether the shape function is differentiable is a long-standing question in this area, so a result settling it in a broad setting is of interest to specialists in growth models. The text does not say how it connects to wider applications, and the use of an AI-assisted, machine-checked proof is noted as a feature of the work.
summary.background:
- Last-passage percolation: a random growth model where you find the path from a corner to a far point that collects the largest total of random weights placed on sites.
- i.i.d. weights: each site's weight is drawn independently from the same distribution.
- Shape function: the limiting growth rate in each direction, which describes the typical size of the maximum-weight path as a function of direction.
- Differentiable: smooth, meaning the shape function has a well-defined slope at each point of the open quadrant.
- Moment assumption: a condition that the weights' tails are not too heavy, measured by finite moments of a given order.
- Percolation cone: a set of directions already handled by known results, so only directions outside it need proof.
- Van den Berg–Kesten inequality: a probability bound on the chance of two events occurring disjointly.
- Lean: a computer proof assistant used to check that a proof is fully correct.

papers.abstract: We prove that the shape function of planar directed last-passage percolation with general i.i.d.\ real-valued weights is differentiable on the open first quadrant, under a moment assumption of order $p''>4$ on the positive part of the weight and a nearly optimal order $p'>1$ on the negative part. Due to known results, only directions outside a percolation cone need be considered. The proof is a multiscale path-counting argument that uses the shape theorem, oriented percolation on a coarse-grained lattice, a simple change of measure in a finite region, and the van den Berg--Kesten inequality. Our Lean-formalized proof is an AI-assisted adaptation and improvement of the OpenAI proof of differentiability in planar first-passage percolation.

papers.title: Besicovitch Pseudo Almost Periodic Stochastic Processes and Their Applications to Delayed Stochastic Neural Networks
papers.label: arXiv:2611.33209v1

summary.one_liner: The paper defines Besicovitch pseudo almost periodic stochastic processes and uses them to study solutions in distribution and their p-th mean stability for delayed stochastic neural networks whose parameters, apart from the time delays, are pseudo almost periodic.
summary.plain: The paper is about systems whose random behaviour repeats in a loose, approximate rhythm, the way a noisy seasonal signal might. It introduces a formal definition for such random processes under a weaker notion of repetition (the Besicovitch sense), then applies it to a model of neural networks that have time delays and random noise. The authors state that they establish existence of such solutions and stability criteria for them.
summary.why: The work extends a mathematical framework for describing oscillating behaviour in randomly driven systems, which may matter for modelling neural networks and similar stochastic dynamical systems. The text does not show applications beyond this theoretical setting, so its practical reach is unclear.
summary.background:
- Almost periodic function: a function that is not exactly periodic but returns arbitrarily close to its earlier patterns at regular-ish intervals.
- Pseudo almost periodic: almost periodic apart from a small part that decays over time.
- Besicovitch sense: a way of measuring closeness on average over long stretches, which is looser than requiring closeness at every moment.
- Stochastic process: a quantity that evolves randomly over time.
- Solution in distribution: describes the statistical behaviour of a random solution rather than one exact path.
- Delayed neural network: a network model in which signals take time to pass between units.
- p-th mean stability: stability measured through the average of the p-th power of the deviation, which is a standard way to measure random errors.

papers.abstract: The Besicovitch almost periodic concept is a generalization of the Bohr, Stepanov, and Weyl almost periodic concepts and, in a certain sense, has broader coverage and weaker conditions. However, the concept of pseudo almost periodic stochastic processes in the Besicovitch sense has not yet been systematically proposed, which limits the characterization of the complex oscillatory behavior of a broader class of stochastic non-autonomous systems. This paper proposes the concept of Besicovitch pseudo almost periodic stochastic processes. As an application of this concept, we study the existence of Besicovitch pseudo almost periodic solutions in distribution for a class of stochastic delayed neural networks in which all parameters except the time delays are pseudo almost periodic and establish stability criteria for such solutions in the $p$-th mean sense. The work of this paper fills the gap caused by the lack of the concept of Besicovitch pseudo almost periodic stochastic processes and provides a new conceptual tool and analytical approach for characterizing the complex oscillatory behavior of stochastic differential equations and stochastic neural network systems.

papers.title: Converse comparison of $g$-expectations and uniqueness of generators of BSDEs: a novel approach and some sharp results
papers.label: arXiv:2611.34304v1

summary.background:
- Stochastic differential equation (SDE): an equation describing a quantity that evolves randomly over time, like a noisy price path.
- Backward SDE (BSDE): an equation run backward from a known terminal value, whose solution includes a random process and a "generator" that sets how the value changes over time.
- Generator: the rule inside a BSDE that determines how the solution drifts; it is the object the paper tries to recover.
- g-expectation: a nonlinear way of averaging a future payoff, defined as the initial value of a BSDE with generator g.
- Comparison theorem: a result saying that if terminal outcomes are ordered, the initial values are ordered too; the converse asks whether the reverse holds.
- Lipschitz condition: a mild smoothness requirement that the rule changes at a bounded rate.
- Uniqueness of generators: the claim that the initial values determine the generator.
summary.one_liner: The paper studies inverse problems for backward stochastic differential equations (BSDEs), proving via a forward-SDE representation of generators that an ordering between two g-expectations forces pointwise comparability of their generators under only the standard Lipschitz assumption, which also yields a general uniqueness theorem for BSDE generators.
summary.plain: The paper asks a reverse question about a mathematical tool called a backward stochastic differential equation, which is used to price risk and model decisions under uncertainty. Given only the final outcomes, can you recover the rule that produced them? The authors show that if one such outcome is always ordered above another, the underlying rules must also be ordered at every point, and they do this without the extra simplifying assumptions earlier work needed.
summary.why: The result claims to fully settle the converse comparison problem for g-expectations in the standard Lipschitz setting, and to give a general uniqueness statement for BSDE generators. Its significance rests on the proofs in the full paper, which the summary does not show; its links to applications in finance or control are not described in the text.

papers.abstract: This paper investigates inverse problems for backward stochastic differential equations (BSDEs), with a particular focus on the converse comparison theorem and the uniqueness of generators solely through the initial values of the corresponding solutions. To this end, we develop a forward-SDE representation approach that combines a contradiction argument with a representation of generators in terms of solutions to associated forward stochastic differential equations (SDEs). As one of the main consequences, we prove that an ordering between two $g$-expectations necessarily implies the pointwise comparability of their generators, without requiring any additional structural assumptions beyond the standard Lipschitz condition. This removes the continuity, $y$-independence, and deterministic assumptions required in previous works, thereby yielding a complete solution to the converse comparison problem for $g$-expectations under the standard Lipschitz framework and, at the same time, establishing a general uniqueness theorem for generators of BSDEs.

papers.title: Graphon hitting times: connectivity and minimum degree
papers.label: arXiv:2611.33540v1

summary.background:
- Random graph: a network whose edges are chosen at random; here edges are added one by one in random order.
- Hitting time: the first moment a property (here, connectivity or having no isolated vertex) holds.
- Graphon: a limiting description of a large random network in which each pair of node "types" has a link probability.
- Degree: the number of links at a node; the degree distribution describes how degrees are spread across nodes.
- Asymptotically almost surely (a.a.s.): with probability tending to 1 as the network grows.
- Laplace transform and vague convergence: standard analytic tools for handling distributions of small values; no need to master them to grasp the main message.
summary.one_liner: The paper proves that, for graphon-based inhomogeneous random graphs under a connectivity and low-degree-tail condition, the connectivity and minimum-degree-one hitting times coincide whp, and gives criteria for when this transition is sharp, using Laplace transforms and vague convergence of rescaled degree measures.
summary.plain: Imagine building a random network one link at a time until every node is connected to the rest. A classic fact for the simplest random networks is that this moment arrives exactly when the last lonely, unlinked node gets its first link. This paper proves a version of that fact for a much broader family of random networks, where different nodes have different chances of linking, described by a "graphon."
summary.why: It extends a well-known random-graph result to inhomogeneous networks, with conditions stated in terms of the graphon's degree distribution. The text also revisits minimum-degree results of Hladký and Viswanathan with simpler proofs, so it may matter to people studying random network models more generally.

papers.abstract: A classical result in random graphs states that the Erd\H{o}s--R\'enyi random graph process becomes connected at exactly the moment its last isolated vertex disappears. The main goal of this paper is to establish a graphon analogue of this result. Let $G(n,W)$ be the inhomogeneous random graph sampled from a graphon $W$, and reveal its edges one by one in a uniformly random order. We prove that if $W$ is connected and the lower tail of its degree distribution satisfies $g_W(t)/t\to 0$ as $t\to 0$, which is needed for the connectivity of $G(n,W)$, then the connectivity and minimum-degree-one hitting times coincide asymptotically almost surely. We also determine when this hitting time occurs at scale $\Theta(n\log n)$, as in the binomial random graph model. Moreover, we give a simple analytic criterion for the transition to be localized in a $(1+o(1))$-multiplicative window, and construct graphons with minimum degrees arbitrarily close to zero whose transition is nevertheless sharp. Our approach uses Laplace transforms and vague convergence of rescaled graphon degree measures to provide a unified framework for analyzing low-degree vertices and connectivity transitions. Along the way, we revisit the minimum degree of~$G(n,W)$, giving simplified proofs of results of Hladk\'y and Viswanathan~\cite{HV} and establishing the limiting distribution of $\delta(G(n,W))$ under a second-order decorrelation condition.

papers.title: Sharp estimates for incremental moments of inverse subordinators and approximation errors for time-changed stochastic differential equations
papers.label: arXiv:2611.33075v1

summary.background:
- Stochastic differential equation: a equation describing a quantity that evolves with random noise, such as a jittery price or particle path.
- Subordinator: a random process that only moves forward in time, built from random jumps; it can act as a random clock.
- Inverse subordinator: the "inverse" of such a clock, which counts how far real time has advanced relative to the random clock; it has flat stretches and is used to model subdiffusion, i.e. slowed-down random motion.
- Time change: substituting a random clock for ordinary time in a process.
- Incremental moments: averages of powers of how much a random quantity changes over a time interval, used to measure size of fluctuations.
- Order of convergence: how quickly the approximation error shrinks as the time step gets smaller.
- Deterministic time grid: approximation computed at fixed, evenly or predefined time points.
summary.one_liner: The paper proves sharp upper and lower bounds on the incremental moments of inverse subordinators and uses them to derive an error bound, shown to be optimal in general, for numerically approximating stochastic differential equations time-changed by an inverse subordinator.
summary.plain: The paper studies a random "clock" that runs slow and jumpy, used to model processes that move more slowly than usual, such as diffusion through a crowded medium. It establishes precise limits on how much this random clock can change over a short stretch of time. These limits are then used to bound the error when computers approximate such time-changed random processes on a fixed grid of time steps.
summary.why: Numerical methods for these time-changed models need reliable error guarantees, and the paper gives one and shows the resulting convergence rate cannot be improved in general. The text does not say which specific applications it targets beyond subdiffusion modelling, so the broader impact is unclear from this abstract alone.

papers.abstract: This paper establishes precise upper and lower bounds for the incremental moments of general inverse subordinators. Such processes are used as random time changes to model subdiffusive phenomena. The upper and lower bounds provide the foundation for a general framework for analyzing numerical approximation of time-changed stochastic differential equations on deterministic time grids. We derive an upper bound for the approximation error and further prove that the resulting order of convergence cannot be improved in general.

papers.title: Temporal Inhomogeneous Random Graphs
papers.label: arXiv:2611.32717v1

summary.one_liner: Extends results on temporal stochastic block models to graphon-based random graphs with a continuous, strictly positive kernel, studying increasing-path reachability and path-length asymptotics in the sparse regime of connection probabilities of order log n / n with uniformly random edge timestamps.
summary.plain:
This paper studies random networks where each pair of nodes is linked with a chance that depends on their positions in a population, and every link gets a random time stamp. It asks how far one can travel from a starting point if each step must use links with strictly later time stamps. The authors find the first-order (leading-order, large-network) size of the set of nodes reachable this way from a fixed node, and the leading-order lengths of the longest and shortest such time-respecting routes.</plain>
<parameter name="why">Time-respecting routes matter for modeling how things spread through contact networks, where order of contacts changes what can reach whom. The text only motivates this via time-dependent propagation in inhomogeneous populations; it does not show specific applications, so the practical reach is unclear from the abstract alone.</why>
<parameter name="background">- Random graph: a network whose links are created by chance; here n is the number of nodes.
- Graphon: a continuous function describing how likely two "types" of nodes are to connect; it generalizes block models where nodes fall into groups.
- Stochastic block model: a random network with a few groups, with link chances depending on group membership.
- Increasing path: a route through the network whose link time stamps strictly increase at each step.
- Log n / n scaling: connection chances sparse enough that each node has on the order of log n links, a regime near where the network becomes connected.
- First-order asymptotics: the leading term describing how a quantity grows as n becomes large.</background>
<parameter name="difficulty">research-level

papers.abstract: Motivated by the study of time-dependent propagation processes in inhomogeneous populations, we extend Burova, Lugosi and Perarnau's results on the temporal stochastic block model to graphon-based random graphs with a continuous and strictly positive kernel. We consider such a graph in the regime where connection probabilities are of the order of $\log n/n$, and equip its edges with a uniformly random ordering, interpreted as timestamps. We study the size of reachable sets via increasing paths (that is, paths whose edge timestamps are strictly increasing). We establish tight first-order asymptotics for the size of the reachable set from a fixed vertex, and also determine the first-order asymptotics of the lengths of the longest and shortest increasing paths with one or two fixed endpoints.

papers.title: Epidemic random model under vaccination regime and non-permanent immunity driven by time-changed Levy noise
papers.label: arXiv:2611.28254v1

summary.background:
- Compartmental epidemic models: populations split into Susceptible, Infected, Recovered, Vaccinated groups, linked by differential equations.
- Basic reproduction number: the average number of new infections caused by one case in a fully susceptible population; above a threshold the disease can spread.
- Non-permanent immunity: recovered or vaccinated people can become susceptible again after immunity wears off.
- Stochastic differential equations: equations with a random noise term, used for quantities that fluctuate unpredictably.
- Lévy noise: random fluctuations that can include both smooth wiggles (Brownian motion) and sudden jumps (Poisson-type events).
- Time change: running the randomness on a random clock, so activity can speed up or slow down.
- Extinction vs. persistence in mean: whether the disease dies out, or its average level stays above zero over the long run.
summary.one_liner: A stochastic SIRV epidemic model with waning (non-permanent) immunity and variable population size, where the contact rate is a random process driven by time-changed Lévy noise, is shown to have a unique positive global solution, a random basic reproduction number, and sufficient conditions for disease extinction and persistence in mean.
summary.plain: This paper studies how a contagious disease might spread in a population when the rate of contact between people fluctuates unpredictably over time. The model splits people into groups (susceptible, infected, recovered, and vaccinated), and immunity from infection or vaccination can wear off. The authors prove the model has a sensible, always-nonnegative solution and give conditions under which the disease dies out or lingers on average, expressed in terms of the model's parameters and two long-run measures.
summary.why: Real contact rates are rarely constant, so models that let them fluctuate randomly are a more realistic way to ask whether an outbreak will fade out. The text does not say how the results compare with data or other models, so their practical use is unclear from the summary alone.

papers.abstract: A random version of the Susceptible-Infected-Recovered-Vaccinated (SIRV) epidemic model with non-permanent immunity and a population of non-constant size is studied. The compartments satisfy a system of differential equations in which the contact rate is a random coefficient, and the contact rate itself is driven by a stochastic differential equation with time-changed Levy noise. This noise is constructed from a conditional Brownian motion and a doubly stochastic Poisson random field, both governed by a stochastic clock. When the clock is independent of the Brownian and Poisson components, the two parts of the noise are a time-changed Brownian motion and a time-changed Poisson random measure. The equation for the contact rate decouples from the compartment equations and enters them as a random parameter, which allows the compartments to be treated pathwise. The existence, uniqueness, and positivity of the global solution are proven, and the basic reproduction number of the model is shown to be random. Furthermore, sufficient conditions for extinction and persistence in mean of the disease are derived. The conditions are expressed in terms of the parameters of the model and two long-run characteristics.

papers.title: Regularity of invariant measures of solutions for fractional stochastic partial differential equations with memory and nonlinear noise
papers.label: arXiv:2611.29406v1

summary.background:
- Stochastic PDE: a partial differential equation driven by random noise.
- Fractional operator: a generalised derivative of non-integer order, used to model nonlocal or anomalous behaviour.
- Memory (non-Markovian) effect: the current evolution depends on the whole past, not just the present state.
- Multiplicative noise: the random disturbance's strength depends on the current state.
- Markov semigroup and invariant measure: the probability distribution a random system settles into and keeps over time.
- Dafermos method: a standard trick that replaces the past history with an auxiliary variable to remove memory.
- Galerkin approximation and Minty's technique: standard tools for proving well-posedness of nonlinear equations.
- Krylov-Bogoliubov approach: a classical way to construct invariant measures from time averages.
summary.one_liner: Proves existence and regularity of invariant measures for stochastic fractional PDEs with memory and nonlinear multiplicative noise, using a Dafermos-type past-history variable to restore a Markov structure.
summary.plain: This paper studies random evolution equations that depend on both their past and random disturbances, the kind used to model materials or processes with memory. The authors recast the problem using a new variable that sums up the past history, which makes the system behave Markov-style, meaning the future depends only on the present state. Using that device, they show that long-run statistical equilibria (invariant measures) exist and that these equilibria have additional smoothness.
summary.why: Long-term behaviour of random systems with memory is hard to analyse because the usual Markov tools fail, so a workable reformulation is of interest to specialists in stochastic PDEs. The text does not discuss applications, so any connection to particular physical or engineering models is not stated here.

papers.abstract: We are concerned with stochastic fractional partial differential equations involving memory and nonlinear multiplicative noise. Based on the well-known Dafermos method, a suitable variable defined by the integrated past history is introduced. This transformation not only overcomes the non-Markovianity of the original problem which prevents us from analyzing invariant measures for the associated Markov semigroup, but also facilitates the analysis of the well-posedness together with the Faedo-Galerkin approximations and Minty's technique. Moreover, we prove the existence of invariant measures by the classical Krylov-Bogoliubov approach, and further establish the regularity of invariant measures by virtue of a control argument.

papers.title: Stochastic Differential Equations on the Simplex
papers.label: arXiv:2611.27309v1

summary.background:
- Simplex: the set of non-negative numbers that sum to one (e.g., proportions of a whole).
- Brownian motion: the mathematical model of continuous random jiggling, as in pollen particles in water.
- Stochastic differential equation (SDE): an equation describing how a quantity changes over time with both a steady push (drift) and random noise.
- Diffusion process: a random process whose solution is described by such an SDE.
- Weak vs. strong solution: a weak solution exists in some probabilistic sense; a strong solution is defined pathwise on a given noise source.
- Pathwise uniqueness: for a given noise path, there is only one solution.
- Jacobi process: a known diffusion living on an interval, here generalised to the simplex.
summary.one_liner: The paper builds a class of simplex-valued diffusion processes as solutions to stochastic differential equations driven by antisymmetric Brownian motion, covering multivariate Jacobi processes and general simplex polynomial diffusions, and proves weak existence plus global strong existence and pathwise uniqueness from strictly positive starting states under a boundary non-attainment condition.
summary.plain: This paper studies random processes that move around inside a simplex, meaning a set of numbers that are all non-negative and add up to one, like a split of a whole into shares. The authors describe such moving shares as solutions to a type of random-motion equation, using a specific kind of random noise that keeps the total fixed. They show that these processes exist and are uniquely determined when they start with every share strictly positive, under a stated condition that they never reach the edge of the simplex.
summary.why: Shares that evolve randomly over time, such as portfolio weights or population proportions, are a natural setting for these models, so a general, well-posed framework matters for that kind of modelling. The text does not discuss applications, so any link to specific fields is my inference rather than something the paper states.

papers.abstract: We propose a framework for simplex-valued diffusion processes, formulated as solutions to stochastic differential equations driven by antisymmetric Brownian motion. Our edge-wise representation includes the multivariate Jacobi processes and the general class of continuous simplex-valued polynomial diffusions. Also, it allows bounded, locally Lipschitz state-dependent drift rates and edge weights. We establish weak solutions, as well as global strong existence and pathwise uniqueness for strictly positive initial states under a sufficient boundary non-attainment condition.

papers.title: Isolation in Random Graphs
papers.label: arXiv:2611.26781v1

summary.background:
- A random graph G(n,p): n vertices, each pair joined by an edge independently with probability p.
- "Asymptotic" / "with high probability": statements about what happens as n grows large, holding with probability tending to 1.
- Domination number γ(G): the fewest vertices that together touch or include every vertex (each vertex is chosen or adjacent to a chosen one).
- Isolation number ι(G): the fewest vertices whose removal leaves a graph with no edges; the paper's F-isolation generalises this to leaving a graph with no copy of F, where F is a fixed forest (F = an edge gives ordinary isolation).
- Two-point concentration: the value is, with high probability, one of two adjacent integers.
- Minimum degree bound: a classical lower bound on domination in terms of the smallest number of neighbours any vertex has.
- Probability asymptotics, including log and little-o notation.
summary.one_liner: Studies the isolation number, domination number and F-isolation of the binomial random graph G(n,p) for p = o(1) and np → ∞, giving two-point concentration results, a transition in the gap between domination and isolation, and asymptotic sharpness of the minimum-degree bound for regular hosts.
summary.plain: This paper looks at random networks where each possible link between n points appears independently with some small probability p. It asks how few "chosen" vertices are needed so that every other vertex is either chosen or next to a chosen one, and how that changes when the goal is weakened to leaving behind only vertices that do not contain a given shape (such as a tree-like pattern). The authors give fairly precise answers on how these numbers behave as the network grows, and show how the gap between two related counts depends on how sparse the network is.
summary.why: These are questions about how precisely typical large random networks can be covered or dominated, and the text reports sharp thresholds where the behaviour of this gap changes. The text does not say what applications it may have, so its wider relevance is unclear from the abstract alone.

papers.abstract: We study isolation in the binomial random graph $G(n,p)$. When $p=o(1)$ and $np\to\infty$, allowing an $F$-free graph on the undominated vertices gives the same first-order asymptotics for every fixed forest $F$ as the domination number $\gamma(G)$ in $G(n,p)$. For the ordinary isolation number $\iota(G)$ ($F$ is an edge) we prove two-point concentration when $p$ is bounded away from $1$ and $np^2/(\log n)^3\to\infty$. We also identify a transition in the gap $\gamma(G)-\iota(G)$ when $\log(1/p)=o(\log n)$. This gap tends to infinity in probability when $p$ is well below $(\log\log n/\log n)^2$ and is at most one with high probability when $p$ is well above this scale. Finally, for every fixed graph $F$, we show that the classical minimum degree bound for domination is asymptotically sharp for $F$-isolation, even for regular host graphs.

papers.title: Generic arm separation for planar percolation models
papers.label: arXiv:2611.26458v1

summary.background:
- Percolation: random open/closed sites or edges on a grid; at the critical point, large connected clusters appear but only just.
- Arm events: the event that several disjoint open or closed paths reach from a point out to a distance, with a given color pattern.
- Quasi-multiplicativity: arm probabilities over different scales multiply up to constant factors, which lets one compare them across scales.
- RSW (Russo–Seymour–Welsh) estimates: bounds that stop open crossings from becoming too unlikely in a box, a basic input to such arguments.
- Universal arm exponents: scaling exponents that depend only on the arm pattern, not on the specific model.
- FK-percolation: a random cluster model linking percolation to the Potts model in physics.
summary.one_liner: A generic arm-separation statement for arbitrary planar percolation models, proved via a model-independent exploration algorithm, with a strong arm-separation result applied to critical planar FK-percolation.
summary.plain: This paper is about random patterns of connected and disconnected regions on a flat plane, the sort of thing that models how fluid seeps through a porous material. The authors prove a general rule saying that several separate paths ("arms") running out from a point can be kept apart from one another in a controlled way, and they show that the rule works for a broad class of such models. They then apply it to a specific model called critical FK-percolation, which is closely tied to statistical physics.
summary.why: Tools like arm separation are standard steps for deriving precise exponents that describe how likely such paths are at the critical point, so a result that holds for any planar model rather than one at a time is useful to researchers in this area. The text does not say how far the result extends beyond the cases it treats, so its wider reach is uncertain.

papers.abstract: Arm separation is an important technical tool in the study of critical and near-critical planar percolation systems. When combined with RSW estimates, it proves quasi-multiplicativity of arm-event probabilities, links the derivatives of different events and allows the identification of universal arm exponents. We provide a very generic statement of arm separation that applies to arbitrary planar percolation models. Our argument is based on exploring configurations conditioned on the existence of arms in such a way that "exposed" arms are revealed with positive probability. The exploration algorithm is independent of the percolation model and applies to all polychromatic arm events. As an application, we prove a strong arm-separation result for critical planar FK-percolation.

papers.title: Dynamical edge universality and the Airy$_β$ line ensemble
papers.label: arXiv:2611.25364v1

summary.background:
- Interacting particle system: many random particles whose motion depends on the others, here with a repulsion parameter β>0.
- Dyson Brownian motion: eigenvalues of a random matrix evolving in time, the standard model of repelling particles.
- Edge universality: the statement that local behavior at the extreme edge of a particle cloud does not depend on fine details of the model.
- Airy line ensemble: a family of random curves (for β=1,2,4 tied to classical random matrix ensembles) describing the edge after rescaling.
- Stieltjes transform: an analytic tool that encodes the particle density; loop equations are identities used to control it.
- Square-root edge: the density vanishes like the square root of distance at the boundary of the cloud.
- Uniform convergence on compact time intervals: the convergence holds uniformly over bounded time windows.
summary.one_liner: The paper proves that three families of interacting particle systems (β-Dyson Brownian motion with analytic potential, weighted β-corners processes, and a class of discrete-time Markov chains), for every β>0, have their top particles near the moving edge converge to the Airy_β line ensemble at positive times, starting from general non-equilibrium initial data.
summary.plain: The paper studies systems of many randomly moving particles that repel each other, and asks what the leading particles at the edge look like over time. It shows that, for three broad families of such systems, once the particle density has a regular square-root shape at its edge, the top few particles, zoomed in on the right scale in space and time, follow a single universal family of random curves called the Airy_β line ensemble. The text indicates this holds regardless of how the system started.
summary.why: Universality results like this explain why very different random systems show the same edge behavior, and the Airy line ensembles are central objects in random matrix theory and probability. The text does not spell out wider applications, so any connection beyond this area is uncertain.

papers.abstract: We prove dynamical edge universality for three families of interacting particle systems for every $β>0$: $β$-Dyson Brownian motion with an analytic potential, weighted $β$-corners processes, and a class of discrete-time Markov chains. Our results apply to general non-equilibrium initial data and show that the Airy$_β$ line ensemble emerges at positive times whenever the limiting density has a regular square-root edge. More precisely, after centering at the moving deterministic edge and rescaling space and time on the $n^{-2/3}$ and $n^{-1/3}$ scales, respectively, the trajectories of the top $k$ particles converge jointly in distribution to the top $k$ curves of the Airy$_β$ line ensemble, for every fixed $k$, in the topology of uniform convergence on compact time intervals. The proof combines dynamical loop equations with characteristic-flow estimates to establish local laws near the moving edge and upper bounds on the extremal particle. We then identify the stochastic evolution of every subsequential limit of the rescaled Stieltjes transform and establish convergence through the pole-evolution characterization of the Airy$_β$ line ensemble.

papers.title: Convergence of replicator-mutator particle systems via bounded Wasserstein distance
papers.label: arXiv:2611.24472v1

summary.background:
- A PDE (partial differential equation) describes how a quantity, here a population density, changes smoothly over space and time.
- Replicator-mutator dynamics: a model where individuals grow or shrink according to fitness (selection) and occasionally change type (mutation, modeled as diffusion).
- Empirical measure: the distribution formed by placing a point mass at each particle's location.
- Wasserstein distance: a way to measure how far apart two probability distributions are, by the cost of moving mass from one to the other.
- Coupling: a way of pairing up particles from two systems so their distance can be bounded.
- Resampling: duplicating particles with high weight and discarding low-weight ones, here done so the particles end up unweighted.
summary.one_liner: The paper derives quantitative error bounds for how closely an unweighted interacting particle system with resampling tracks the solution of a replicator-mutator PDE, using a bounded-cost Wasserstein-1 distance to handle unbounded potentials on an unbounded state space.
summary.plain: This paper looks at a system of many randomly moving "particles" that are duplicated or removed depending on how well they fit an external landscape, and asks how well their overall distribution matches a smooth mathematical equation describing the same process. The authors measure the mismatch with a distance between probability distributions and prove explicit error estimates for it. The text indicates the approach works even when the landscape values are unbounded and the space is unbounded.
summary.why: Particle systems of this kind appear in evolutionary biology, optimization methods and particle filtering, so error bounds for their approximation of a continuous equation are useful for justifying such methods. The text does not discuss specific applications or compare results to prior work, so its wider significance is not established from the excerpt alone.

papers.abstract: Interacting particle systems with selection and mutation mechanisms arise in biological modeling, evolutionary optimization, and particle filtering methods. In this work we will consider the paradigmatic replicator-mutator PDE, which combines a diffusive component with a source term that depends on an external potential. We derive quantitative error estimates for the distance between the empirical measure of an unweighted particle system and the solution of the PDE. The proof uses a Wasserstein-1 distance with a bounded ground cost, which allows us to treat unbounded potentials on an unbounded state space. The key tools are the optimal coupling of newly resampled particles and, for the time-continuous limit, the use of a discrete-time killing resampling.

papers.title: Parameter estimation for discretely observed rough fractional interacting particle systems
papers.label: arXiv:2611.24287v1

summary.background:
- Fractional Brownian motion: a random path like Brownian motion, but with memory; the Hurst parameter H controls its roughness (H = 1/2 is ordinary Brownian motion).
- Interacting particle system / McKean-Vlasov equation: many particles whose motion depends on the average behaviour of the group; propagation of chaos means that as the group grows, particles behave increasingly independently, each like a single representative particle.
- Contrast estimator / least squares: a parameter estimate found by minimising a fit criterion built from the observed data.
- Consistency: the estimate converges to the true value as data grow. Asymptotic normality: the estimation error, rescaled, approaches a bell-shaped distribution.
- Stochastic sewing lemma: a tool for controlling sums of rough random increments.
- Quadratic variation: a sum of squared increments over a fine grid, used to estimate noise scale and roughness.
summary.one_liner: Parameter estimation for a system of interacting particles driven by fractional Brownian motions, using discrete observations of all particles, with consistency and asymptotic normality results for the drift parameter in the joint limit of many particles and vanishing observation mesh, including a rough regime H in (1/4, 1/2).
summary.plain: The paper studies how to estimate an unknown tuning value that governs how a large group of randomly moving particles drifts, when we can only watch their positions at discrete moments in time. The particles are pushed by correlated, rough random noise and also influence each other. The authors build estimators, prove they become accurate and behave like a normal distribution as the number of particles grows and the time gaps between observations shrink, and add a procedure that also estimates the noise's roughness and scale.
summary.why: Estimating parameters from coarse, noisy snapshots of many interacting systems is a basic problem in statistics applied to physics, biology and finance-style models. The text reports that the rate of convergence in the observation spacing changes at H = 3/4, which is a specific technical finding; its wider relevance beyond this model class is not shown in the text.

papers.abstract: We study parametric inference for interacting particle systems driven by independent fractional Brownian motions, based on discrete observations of all particles over a fixed time horizon. Our goal is to estimate an unknown drift parameter in the joint limit as the number of particles increases and the observation mesh vanishes. For $H>\frac 12$, we construct contrast based estimators by extending the discrete time least squares approach of Neuenkirch and Tindel to the interacting setting. For the rough regime $H\in(\frac 14,\frac 12)$, we introduce a modified contrast and use the stochastic sewing lemma to handle the first order approximations available from discrete observations. Our analysis combines the propagation of chaos for the associated fractional McKean Vlasov equation with estimates controlling the temporal discretization error. When the Hurst parameter and the diffusion coefficient are known, we establish strong consistency and asymptotic normality of the proposed estimators. The asymptotic results reveal an interplay between the number of particles and the temporal discretization: the convergence rate with respect to the observation mesh changes at $H=\frac 34$, while the asymptotic normality holds in both regimes considered. We further develop a joint estimation procedure for the drift parameter, the Hurst parameter, and the diffusion coefficient, extending quadratic-variation methods for fractional Brownian motion to the interacting particle framework. Numerical experiments illustrate the performance of the proposed estimators.

papers.title: Uniform spatial Schauder estimates for backward stochastic partial differential equations with random coefficients
papers.label: arXiv:2611.22285v1

summary.background:
- Backward stochastic PDE: a partial differential equation running backward in time with a random driving term (a martingale, a process whose expected future value equals its present value).
- Schauder estimate: a bound saying that if the equation's inputs are smooth enough, the solution is also smooth enough, with control on its derivatives.
- Super-parabolic: a parabolic equation with extra diffusion strength, so heat-like smoothing is strong.
- Heat-kernel bounds: estimates of how heat spreads from a point over time, used to control solutions.
- Conditional energy norm: a size measure for functions that is averaged given the information available at each time.
- Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation: a nonlinear equation giving the optimal value in a control problem; the stochastic version adds randomness.
- Uniform in probability: the bound holds for all random outcomes, not just typical ones.
summary.one_liner: The paper proves spatial Schauder estimates, uniform in probability and time, for super-parabolic backward stochastic PDEs with random space-time coefficients, using a weighted conditional energy norm, and applies them to semilinear stochastic HJB equations.
summary.plain: The paper studies a type of random equation that runs backward in time and changes from one moment to the next, the kind that arises when controlling systems under uncertainty. The authors prove bounds that control how smooth the solution is in space, and these bounds hold for every random outcome and at every time rather than only on average. They then use these bounds to show that a certain family of nonlinear control equations (stochastic Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equations) has solutions of this smooth kind.
summary.why: Estimates of this kind are the tools that let mathematicians show a random equation has a well-behaved solution, which matters for stochastic control and related optimisation problems. The text does not say how widely the method will extend beyond the stated setting, so its broader reach is uncertain.

papers.abstract: We prove spatial Schauder estimates for super-parabolic backward stochastic partial differential equations. All coefficients can be random and depend on time and space, and the estimates are uniform in probability and time. The key ingredient is a weighted conditional energy norm adapted to the parabolic scale of each frequency block. Together with heat-kernel bounds and coefficient freezing, it controls the gradient-martingale coupling without assuming a bounded martingale integrand. As an application, we establish Schauder solvability for semilinear stochastic Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman equations.

papers.title: Quantum Monge-Kantorovich optimal transport in spacetime through spatiotemporal Kirkwood-Dirac distributions and spatiotemporal states
papers.label: arXiv:2611.23462v1

summary.background:
- Optimal transport: finding the cheapest way to reshape one probability distribution into another, with a cost function.
- Wasserstein distance: a standard way to measure how far apart two distributions are under this cost.
- Density operator: the quantum analogue of a probability distribution, describing a quantum system's state.
- Quasiprobability distribution: a probability-like function that can take complex or negative values, used in quantum physics.
- Kirkwood-Dirac distribution: a specific quasiprobability built from measurement outcomes at two different times or observables.
- Non-Hermitian operator: a quantum operator that is not equal to its own adjoint, so its values can be complex.
- Operator frame: a generalized set of operators that allows reconstruction of quantum objects without requiring an orthogonal basis.
summary.one_liner: The paper extends quantum optimal transport to spacetime, using spatiotemporal Kirkwood-Dirac quasiprobabilities and spatiotemporal states, and shows the two formalisms are equivalent via operator frames.
summary.plain: The paper is about the best way to move one probability pattern into another at the lowest cost, a problem from mathematics, but now in a quantum setting where time is treated alongside space. The authors build two equivalent versions of this problem, one using complex-valued "quasiprobability" distributions and one using quantum states. They also show that a special real-valued choice (the Margenau-Hill distribution) gives a well-behaved version and define a distance-like measure between such spacetime distributions.
summary.why: Extending optimal transport from space to spacetime is a conceptual step that may matter for quantum measurements where the order of events matters. The text does not show concrete applications or numerical results, so its practical reach is unclear from this abstract alone.

papers.abstract: Monge-Kantorovich optimal transport is a mathematical framework that determines the most efficient way to transform one probability distribution into another while minimizing a given cost function. Its central constructions include the Wasserstein distances, which quantify the space of probability distributions, and dual formulations that link to convex analysis. Its standard quantum generalization replaces probability distributions with density operators and cost function with positive semidefinite cost operator, which should be regarded as spatial quantum optimal transport. In this work, we propose the quantum optimal transport problem in spacetime through the spatiotemporal phase-space Kirkwood-Dirac quasiprobability distribution and spatiotemporal states and through spatiotemporal state. We show that the two formalisms are equivalent and related via spatiotemporal operator frames. In the Kirkwood-Dirac phase-space formalism, the spatiotemporal distribution and the cost function are complex-valued, and the spatiotemporal couplings are Kirkwood-Dirac quasiprobability distributions that yield the correct marginals for the local states. In the spatiotemporal state formalism, the cost operators are generally non-Hermitian, and the spatiotemporal couplings are generally non-Hermitian and yield the correct reduced local states. The Margenau-Hill phase-space distribution gives rise to a real-valued optimal transport in spatiotemporal phase space; in the spatiotemporal state formalism, this corresponds to a Hermitian spatiotemporal coupling state. We give a rigorous definitions and a careful discussion of its duality. We also introduce a spatiotemporal quantum Wasserstein metric based on a metric in spatiotemporal phase spaces and show that it satisfies the metric axioms.

papers.title: The speed of convergence for propagation of chaos in the mean-field Ising model
papers.label: arXiv:2611.17911v1

summary.background:
- Curie–Weiss model: a simple model of magnetism where N spins all interact equally with the average spin.
- Inverse temperature β: a parameter controlling interaction strength; larger β means spins align more strongly. β=1 is the critical point where a phase change begins.
- Propagation of chaos: the statement that k particles in a large interacting system behave nearly independently as the system grows.
- Marginal: the joint distribution of just k of the N spins, ignoring the rest.
- Relative entropy (KL divergence) and chi-square divergence: measures of how different one probability distribution is from another.
- Likelihood ratio: the ratio of the true joint density to the product of independent densities; its correction term carries the dependence.
- Asymptotics / o(·) notation: exact leading-order behaviour as N grows, with the error term small relative to it.
- Quartic law: the limiting distribution of the rescaled magnetization at β=1, and α_c is its second moment.
summary.one_liner: Sharp asymptotics for the relative entropy and chi-square divergence of k-spin marginals in the Curie–Weiss model, showing how fast propagation of chaos occurs for subsystems below, at, and near the critical inverse temperature β=1.
summary.plain: The paper studies a model of many interacting magnets (spins) that each feel the average of all the others. It asks how close a small group of k spins, taken from a large system of N spins, looks to being fully independent of each other, measured by relative entropy (a standard way of scoring how far one probability distribution is from another). The authors give precise formulas for how this distance shrinks as N grows, with separate answers for high, critical, and in-between interaction strengths.
summary.why: The result pins down the exact rate at which the independence of a few particles emerges in a mean-field system, including a change of rate at the critical temperature. The text says the proof works through pair correlations controlling the leading correction to the likelihood ratio, which may be useful for other mean-field or particle-system questions, though the text does not spell out wider applications.

papers.abstract: We derive sharp relative-entropy asymptotics for increasing propagation of chaos in the Curie--Weiss model at zero external field. For every fixed inverse temperature $0<β<1$, the relative entropy of a $k$-spin marginal with respect to the symmetric product measure is $$ \frac{β^2}{4(1-β)^2}\frac{k(k-1)}{N^2}+o\left(\frac{k^2}{N^2}\right),\qquad k=o(N). $$ At the critical inverse temperature $β=1$, the rate changes to $α_{\mathrm c}^2 k(k-1)/(4N)+o(k^2/N)$ in the regime $k=o(\sqrt N)$, where $α_{\mathrm c}$ is the second moment of the limiting quartic law of the rescaled magnetization. We also obtain asymptotics for sequences $β_N\uparrow1$ that interpolate between these two regimes. Crucially, the proof reveals that the pair correlations determine the leading correction to the likelihood ratio, providing precise control of both the chi-square divergence and relative entropy.

papers.title: Local Limit Theorems and Edgeworth Expansions for some classes of inhomogeneous Markov chains
papers.label: arXiv:2611.20233v1

summary.background:
- Markov chain: a random process where the next state depends only on the current state.
- Inhomogeneous: the transition rules change with time (or with a random environment).
- Central limit theorem: sums of random quantities look approximately normal (bell-shaped) when scaled.
- Local limit theorem: a finer version giving approximate probabilities for individual values, not just ranges.
- Edgeworth expansion: correction terms added to the normal approximation to improve accuracy.
- Ellipticity / Doeblin / mixing conditions: technical assumptions saying the chain forgets its past and does not get stuck in restricted moves.
- Diophantine condition: a number-theoretic condition on how well quantities can be approximated by fractions, used to control periodic behavior.
summary.one_liner: The paper proves local limit theorems and Edgeworth expansions for sums of inhomogeneous Markov chains under a one-step lower ellipticity condition, including random-environment and quantum-trajectory settings.
summary.plain: The paper studies sums of values taken along a chain of random steps, where the rules for each step can change over time. Classical limit results say such sums settle into a bell-shaped pattern; this work gives finer statements about how likely each exact value is, and corrections to the bell shape. The authors state that their conditions hold in several settings, including chains driven by random environments and a model of quantum trajectories.
summary.why: The text claims weaker conditions than several earlier results (no two-sided ellipticity, no lower psi-mixing in places), which matters for applying these tools to more models. The connection to quantum trajectories is stated only briefly, so its practical relevance is not clear from the text alone.

papers.abstract: In this note, we prove local central limit theorems and expansions in the central limit theorem for inhomogeneous Markov chains satisfying a one-step lower ellipticity condition. As for the local limit theorem, in the general inhomogeneous case, compared with \cite{DS}, we are able to prove results without two-sided ellipticity, although only in the one-step case. Compared with \cite{PeligradLLT1,PeligradLLT2}, we are able to prove local limit theorems without a lower $ψ$-mixing condition. Concerning Edgeworth expansions, compared with \cite{DHPTRF1}, we are able to get results without two-sided ellipticity (under some sequential Diophantine conditions). Our conditions are then verified for Markov chains in a random dynamical environment with a one-sided Doeblin condition under very mild assumptions. For Markov chains in a random environment, we also consider the more general case of $φ$-mixing chains and then, under some mild periodicity assumptions on the environment, we prove local central limit theorems and first-order Edgeworth expansions (without any ellipticity assumptions), matching the results for deterministic homogeneous chains. When the chain is driven by a topologically mixing subshift of finite type, we obtain high-order expansions for $φ$-mixing chains under some Diophantine conditions of a deterministic system generated by a periodic point. We then apply our results to bounded additive functionals of posterior states in disordered quantum trajectories and establish local central limit theorems and first-order Edgeworth expansions.
